title: Throwing a wide pouring-lip jug
subtitle: Throwing a one-litre jug with a wide pinched spout for drip-free pouring
excerpt: A well-designed jug pours cleanly without dripping down the side. The key is the spout: the lip must be pulled into a wide, flat channel that directs the flow and stops the liquid from wrapping around the jug's surface. This pattern throws a one-litre stoneware jug and details the pinching technique for forming a reliable pouring lip.
sourceNotes: Jug form and pouring lip methodology derived from studio ceramics functional ware practice. Lip-formation technique for drip-free pouring is documented in functional ceramics technical instruction.

glossaryTerms.definition: Working thrown clay until it runs true with no wobble.
The correct drying stage for adding a handle and trimming the foot ring.
A shaped spout formed from the rim of a jug or pitcher that directs liquid flow away from the side of the vessel.

content.text: This pattern requires a pottery wheel and kiln firing to cone 6 (approximately 1220 °C). Use a food-safe mid-fire glaze for the interior and lip area. A handle is attached at leather-hard: the handle attachment and the lip formation both require clean score-and-slip joins.
Jugs fail to pour cleanly for three reasons: the

is too narrow and the flow swells past it; the lip channel is too shallow and liquid wraps sideways; or the rim is too thin and splits the flow. The fix is the same in each case: pinch a wide, deep channel while the clay is still wet. Let it stiffen fully before adding the handle.
Weigh 850 g of smooth stoneware. Wedge and

Pull up the walls in three passes. For a jug, the form opens outward slightly below the rim: bell-shaped, not strictly straight-sided. Target height: 16 to 17 cm tall with a maximum belly diameter of 13 to 14 cm. Wall thickness: 5 to 6 mm. The rim must be slightly thicker: 7 to 8 mm: because clay will be removed when forming the spout.
Compress the rim flat using a chamois cloth or a smooth-edged rib. An even, flat rim is the starting point for a reliable pouring lip.

Stop the wheel. Working with the jug off the bat on a work surface, place the thumb and forefinger of one hand on the rim at the point you want the spout (opposite the eventual handle position). Pinch gently and push the clay outward away from the centre to create a small pout in the rim.

Widen the pout by pressing the inside of the jug with two fingers while holding the outside with the other hand. Push the inside clay gently outward and downward to create a wide, shallow channel: 4 to 5 cm wide at the rim, 2 cm deep. The channel should taper smoothly into the interior of the jug, not end abruptly.

The tip of the pouring lip (the outermost point of the channel) should be narrowed to approximately 2 cm wide: this directs the stream. Do not narrow it further, or the flow will stream off the sides of the lip. A narrow pinch at the very tip is enough.

Test the lip shape: fill the jug with water and pour slowly into a bowl. The stream should leave the lip cleanly and stop immediately when the jug is tilted back. If the water drips down the side, the channel is too shallow: deepen it while the clay is still soft.

, pull a handle from a ball of stoneware clay. Attach it opposite the lip. Score and slip both the upper and lower attachment points. The upper attachment sits 2 cm below the rim. The lower attachment sits 5 to 6 cm above the base. Let the handle dry on the jug before bisque firing.

rows.problem: Liquid drips down the side of the jug after pouring
rows.cause: Channel too shallow; lip tip too wide; rim not thick enough to hold the lip shape through firing
rows.fix: Deepen the channel further while still plastic. Ensure the rim was at least 7 mm thick before forming the lip.

rows.problem: Pouring lip splits into two streams
rows.cause: Tip of the lip pinched to a knife edge with a groove running along it
rows.fix: Pinch the lip tip narrower than the channel but do not create a crease. The tip should be smooth and rounded, not creased.

rows.problem: Handle pulls away from jug at one join during drying
rows.cause: Joins not at matching moisture levels; insufficient slip or scoring
rows.fix: Score both surfaces, apply joining slip to both, and blend the join on the inside of the attachment point with a finger.
